title: THAKRAL: From Holding Company to Growth-and-Value Story?
article:
Thakral Corporation’s investment story is looking less like that of a holding company and more like a company with identifiable growth catalysts.

The group owns a collection of investment assets — notably, its 17% stake in Australia-listed GemLife — but its fast-growing Lifestyle business and the progress of its Gurugram property project are providing investors with clearer development catalysts.

In 9M2026, its Lifestyle business -- which distributes DJI products, branded fragrances and Nespresso -- generated about
S$346 million
of revenue, with segment profit rising
30% to S$16.9 million
.
L-R: CEO Inderbethal Singh Thakral | Independent chairman Lim Swe Guan | Nitin Agarwal, Head, Strategic Investments.

At the same time, Thakral has achieved an important milestone for its 20.7-acre Gurugram development by signing Manipal Hospitals for a major healthcare project.

And management says the structure has substantially reduced Thakral’s development risk.

THAKRAL

Share price:
$1.45

Target:
$2.18

Phillip Securities analyst Darren Chan shares the positive view, maintaining his BUY recommendation after the 3Q update.
His latest report, titled
“Multiple projects underpin growth”
, sets a
S$2.18
target price.
However, he also cut his FY2026 adjusted PATMI forecast by 18% to S$15.0 million, reflecting higher finance costs and lower margins.

Lifestyle growth remains strong

Thakral’s Lifestyle business encompasses DJI products across South Asia, beauty and fragrance distribution in Greater China, Nespresso India and several emerging businesses.

The biggest Lifestyle market remains South Asia, where revenue rose
34.4%
in 9M2026.

Interestingly, the growth story is no longer predominantly about consumer drones.

CEO Inderbethal Singh Thakral said DJI’s business has increasingly shifted towards products used by content creators and influencers, including cameras, gimbals, microphones and related accessories.

“Now everything has pivoted towards the new economy, which is your creators, your KOLs or your influencers.”

The Greater China fragrance business was even stronger, with revenue climbing
41% from S$59.7 million to S$84.4 million
.

Lifestyle remains a relatively low-margin distribution business, however. The S$16.9 million segment profit on S$346 million of revenue implies a segment margin of
4.9%
.

Thus the investment case rests more on sustained revenue growth and scale than on fat margins.
As announced in Sept 2026, Thakral is working to spin off its Lifestyle division, possibly in 1Q2027:

Phillip's analyst values the Lifestyle business at S$258 million, applying a 12-times FY2026 estimated P/E multiple.
That valuation alone is greater than Thakral’s current market capitalisation of about S$208 million.

Phillip’s sum-of-the-parts valuation assigns:

• S$258 million to Lifestyle
• S$225 million to Thakral’s GemLife stake
• S$60 million to The Beauty Tech Group stake
• S$213 million to investment properties.

That gives gross SOTP value of about
S$757 million
. After deducting S$93 million of net debt, Phillip arrives at S$664 million of equity value.

Phillip then applies a hefty
50% conglomerate discount
, resulting in the S$2.18 target price.

Manipal deal de-risks Gurugram

Potentially transformational is Thakral’s Gurugram property project.

The group owns about
20.7 acres in Sector 76 in New Gurugram
, close to the Delhi-Mumbai Highway and planned public transport links.

Management says there are around 36,000 homes in the surrounding area, with roughly 28,000 currently under construction, including major projects by DLF, India’s largest listed property developer.

Thakral believes the rapid residential growth creates demand for social infrastructure, particularly healthcare.

Its solution is a healthcare-led development anchored by Manipal Healthcare Enterprises.

Under a roughly
30-year lease
, Thakral provides the land and development rights, while Manipal is responsible for funding, constructing, obtaining hospital-related approvals and operating the hospital.

The first phase is expected to comprise up to
500 beds
, with scope eventually to add around another 400 beds.

The economics:

Instead of receiving only fixed rent, Thakral will receive a
revenue share subject to a minimum guaranteed rent
.

Nitin Agarwal, Thakral's Head of Strategic Investments, explained:

“We can ride the entire upswing of the healthcare growth that India is witnessing right now.”

Manipal intends the project to become its flagship hospital for Northern India, with Thakral also highlighting the potential for medical tourism given the site's proximity to Delhi’s international airport.

The objective is to balance long-term recurring rental income from healthcare and wellness assets with faster cash generation from residential sales.

Bethal also floated a striking number: residential sales could generate more than
S$300 million of gross sales value
over roughly five to seven years, based on around one million square feet and current market pricing of about S$300 psf.

The amount flowing to Thakral will depend on its revenue-sharing agreement with the residential developer.

Rising debt

Finance costs jumped 71.5% year on year following Thakral’s S$70 million MTN issuance in April.

Thakral’s rising debt has been one concern.

Management provided useful context: around
S$75 million
relates to trust-receipt and working-capital financing for the Lifestyle business, which entered 3Q carrying higher inventory ahead of Diwali, China’s 11/11 sales period, Christmas and Chinese New Year.

If that inventory converts into sales and working-capital requirements fall, borrowings should subsequently fall.

Value unlocking comes into focus

Thakral's investment thesis now rests on several potential value drivers:
Lifestyle growth, upcoming Lifestyle listing, GemLife, Gurugram and Japanese property monetisation
.
Thakral’s proposed spin-off of its Lifestyle business a
ims to establish an independent market value for an operation that is growing revenue at more than 25%.
It is currently buried inside a company containing listed investments, property and private businesses.
CurrentBody is a key brand of the Beauty Tech Group. Its masks which comprise red LED lights are purchased for skin health.
Thakral has just
sold off its stake
in The Beauty Tech Group for S$56.5 million, unlocking capital for its next phase of growth.
The sale reflects an IRR of about 100% since the initial share swap in 2023.
Including S$13.1 million from the partial sale at The Beauty Tech Group’s IPO in London in October 2025, the investment has returned about S$70 million in cash to the Group.
On a pro forma basis, NTA per share rises to
S$2.54
from S$2.42 as at 30 June 2026.

title: REITs vs. Blue-Chip Stocks: Which Offers Better Passive Income on the SGX?
article:
In our first article, “
What Is a Dividend? A Beginner’s Guide to Passive Income in Singapore”,
we learnt what a dividend was and showed you how dividend investing turns your savings into a steady stream of passive income.
On the Singapore Exchange (SGX), two types of dividend payers pop up the most:
real estate investment trusts
(REITs) and blue-chip stocks.
Both can deposit regular cash straight into your bank account, yet they play by completely different rules.
So, which one is actually better for passive income?
Let’s break down how they work so you can figure out what suits your investing style best.
What Are REITs and How Do They Generate Income?
Think of REITs as
collective property ownership
.
Instead of saving up millions to buy a shopfront or a warehouse on your own, a REIT lets you buy units in a massive portfolio of income-producing real estate.
These properties collect rent from corporate tenants.
Once the REIT pays for maintenance, property taxes, and loan interest, the leftover cash is handed out to you – the unitholder – as a distribution per unit (DPU).
Singapore offers a
wide variety
of REITs:
Retail & Commercial:
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, owns household names like Plaza Singapura and Paragon, while
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U) dominates the heartlands with suburban malls like NEX and Causeway Point.
Industrial & Logistics:
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U) owns logistics parks and warehouses across the Asia Pacific.
Healthcare:
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU) owns private hospitals and medical facilities, including Mount Elizabeth and Gleneagles.
To qualify for tax transparency treatment here, Singapore REITs (S-REITs) must distribute at least 90% of their taxable income to unitholders.
That rule is the exact reason REITs are beloved by income hunters.
Still, payouts aren’t guaranteed – if tenants move out or borrowing costs spike, your DPU can take a hit.
What Are Blue-Chip Stocks?
Blue-chip stocks
are the heavyweights of the market – large, household-name businesses with proven track records and deep pockets.
Our blue chips on the Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) span the industries that keep Singapore running day to day:
Banking:
Singapore’s trio of local banks –
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05),
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, and
United Overseas Bank Limited
(SGX: U11), also referred to as UOB, – form the cornerstone of the local market, bringing in profits from mortgages, business loans, credit cards, and wealth management.
Market Infrastructure:
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68) isn’t just where you buy stocks; it’s a listed company itself. As Singapore’s only securities exchange, it enjoys a natural monopoly, collecting steady listing and trading fees whenever markets are active.
Aviation & Engineering:
Singapore Airlines
(SGX: C6L) and
Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd
(SGX: S63), or ST Engineering, earn their keep from global air travel, aerospace maintenance, and defence technology.
Hospitality & Telecoms:
Genting Singapore Limited
(SGX: G13) runs Resorts World Sentosa, while
Singapore Telecommunications
Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, provides regional telecommunications services.
Unlike S-REITs, blue chips aren’t bound by any 90% payout rule.
Management can freely decide how much profit to reinvest into growing the business, paying down debt, or returning to shareholders as a dividend per share (DPS).
That gives them plenty of room to grow, though your dividends generally track the company’s actual profits.
REITs vs. Blue-Chip Stocks: How Do They Compare?
Weighing REITs vs. blue-chip stocks side-by-side makes their trade-offs much easier to spot:
Feature
Singapore REITs
Blue-Chip Stocks
Primary Income Source
Property rental income
Commercial business profits
Payout Type
Distribution Per Unit (DPU)
Dividend Per Share (DPS)
Income Focus
Generally higher yields due to 90% payout rule
Varies depending on business growth plans
Growth Potential
Rental increases and property acquisitions
Expanding operations, pricing power, and rising earnings
Main Risks
High interest rates and tenant vacancies
Market competition and economic shifts
One trap many new investors fall into is chasing the highest yield on the screen.
Remember that your total return comes from
both
the dividends you pocket and how the share price moves over time.
A juicy 8% yield won’t feel like much of a win if the underlying business is struggling and its share price drops by 20%.
Which Is Better for Passive Income?
It really comes down to what you want your money to do for you right now:
Go with REITs if you want higher, property-backed payouts today without dealing with tenants, leaky roofs, or mortgage paperwork.
Choose blue chips if you’re happy with a slightly lower starting yield in exchange for stronger business growth and the potential for long-term capital gains.
But here is something most seasoned dividend investors figure out sooner rather than later: you don’t actually have to pick a side.
Think of REITs and blue chips like teammates playing different positions.
S-REITs do the heavy lifting for immediate rental cash flow, while STI blue chips bring earnings power across banking, telecoms and aviation.
Holding a mix of both keeps your passive income from leaning too heavily on one sector.
If high interest rates squeeze property trusts for a year or two, strong bank dividends can help pick up the slack – and vice versa.
Spreading your capital across property rentals, regional telecommunications, and financial services helps keep your passive income stream steady even if a single industry faces temporary headwinds.
Get Smart: Sustainable Income Wins the Race
Both S-REITs and blue-chip stocks play essential roles in building a reliable stream of cash flow.
The secret to building lasting passive income isn’t about hunting down the single highest yield on the SGX today.
It’s about owning sturdy, reliable businesses that can keep paying you – and ideally raising those payouts – year after year.
Ready to put this into practice?

title: Oil futures swing on fears of escalation in strikes against Iran
article:
(Nov 20) : Oil prices swung amid concern that violence in the Middle East will re-escalate despite pressure on US President Donald Trump to pursue a diplomatic resolution to the nine-month war.

Brent futures settled just below US$92 a barrel after toggling through a roughly US$2 range Thursday. The commodity pared earlier gains after Trump told Axios he was not “rushing into a decision” on Iran.

Meanwhile, the US president’s energy chief played down any anxiety about Mideast supplies, noting that flows through the Strait of Hormuz reached a record.

Earlier Thursday, Western officials said that chances of the US launching another round of mass strikes against Iran appeared to have grown in recent days as the two sides stepped up skirmishes.

Iran, for its part, said it won’t engage on the nuclear weapons issue until the question of the Strait of Hormuz is settled, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.

Oil prices also were buffeted as Trump’s meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts yielded an agreement to ramp up global fuel supplies. The international crude benchmark is down roughly 20% this month following a recovery in supplies from the Persian Gulf.

See also: Stocks fall as Anthropic debut not an AI all-clear

“We are not yet at the point where the narrative of improving supply is enough to overshadow the military flare-ups,” said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank. “Flows through Hormuz have improved, yet ships are still being attacked and President Trump is yet again considering plans for another round of extensive strikes on Iran.”

The International Energy Agency said Thursday that the war could reshape global energy markets for years to come, pushing governments to prioritize reliability and cost after the unprecedented supply shock. It also said that if a resolution were reached soon, both oil and natural gas could turn into buyers’ markets as volumes rise.

For now, traders are wary of betting on the trajectory of the conflict.

See also: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as Anthropic in focus

“Liquidity is poor across the markets, which is understandable after a big drop, which has created opportunities but also a great deal of losses,” said Ole Sloth Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank.

Fuel prices have begun to pull back from a momentous rally that’s fanned inflation fears around the world. European diesel futures slid to a three-month low on Thursday, even as prices remain historically high. Retail gasoline prices have fallen harder as refineries run at full tilt, principally to produce more diesel but making lots of gasoline in the process.

On the demand front, China’s appetite for crude is rebounding faster than expected as lower prices spur refiners to use up import quotas and rebuild stockpiles. Energy Aspects Ltd., FGE NexantECA and Rystad Energy AS have all raised fourth-quarter import forecasts, ranging from 9.8 million to 10.2 million barrels a day.

title: Stocks fall as Anthropic debut not an AI all-clear
article:
(Nov 20) : A rally in stocks fizzled out as Anthropic PBC’s solid market debut failed to sustain enthusiasm for the artificial-intelligence trade.

The sharp reversal drove the S&P 500 down 2%, with the gauge posting its longest slide since April 2024. Shares of the AI lab pared their surge to trade 17% above the IPO price. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. sank on a Hunterbrook Capital short-call that cited China risks. AMD denied any wrongdoing.

Wall Street’s fresh bout of volatility engulfed the broader market, with more than 460 firms in the US equity benchmark retreating. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed on the verge of a technical correction. All megacaps fell.

While Anthropic’s debut was a historic moment for AI, it also took place during an unsettling moment for the industry. Tech stocks have been under pressure as investors question whether the AI boom will ultimately generate returns large enough to justify the industry’s borrowing binge.

“The Anthropic IPO has been a major success,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “However, the IPO does little to address the market’s bigger problems including AI profitability concerns, massive spending, higher interest rates, credit market stress and geopolitical risks.”

The stock began trading Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

See also: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as Anthropic in focus

Anthropic’s IPO is a huge win for the AI trade because it proves investors aren’t running away, which was one of the fears driving the spending slowdown thesis, according to Luke Lango, editor of the Innovation Investor newsletter.

“But don’t mistake one blockbuster deal for an all-clear signal,” he said. “Wall Street writing a check to the world’s leading frontier lab, a company with explosive revenue growth and customers lining up for more, is very different from Wall Street writing checks to debt-heavy neoclouds and the riskier corners of the AI stack.”

The first is a bet on the winner, said Lango. The second is a bet on the buildout, and that’s where money has gotten a lot pickier, he added.

See also: Stocks fall on tech disruptions as Nvidia in focus

With hundreds of billions of dollars committed to infrastructure such as chips and data centers, the next challenge for the top AI labs is to grow revenue fast enough to outpace the industry’s ambitious spending plans.

“Anthropic will need to show that it can expand the use of its models while containing the cost of meeting that demand,” said Antonio Di Giacomo at XS.com.
